title: Devil's Rope Museum
summary: The Texas museum devoted entirely to barbed wire - where 2,000 varieties of 'devil's rope' tell the story of how a simple invention ended the open range, transformed the West, and became the subject of obsessive collectors.

content.intro: In McLean, Texas, along the remnants of Route 66, sits a museum dedicated to the most transformative invention in Western history: barbed wire. The Devil's Rope Museum holds over 2,000 variations of the twisted wire that enclosed the open range, ended the great cattle drives, and made the fencing of the American West possible. For ranchers and farmers, barbed wire was a godsend - cheap, effective fencing that could enclose millions of acres. For cowboys and Native Americans, it was the devil's rope, slicing land into parcels and ending a way of life. For collectors, it became an obsession - antique barbed wire is a serious hobby, with rare varieties commanding hundreds of dollars per strand. The museum in McLean preserves this strange intersection of utility, tragedy, and collecting mania.

sections.title: The Invention
sections.body: Before barbed wire, fencing the West was nearly impossible. There wasn't enough wood for rail fences; hedges took years to grow; smooth wire couldn't contain livestock. In 1874, Joseph Glidden of DeKalb, Illinois, patented his design: two twisted wires with sharp barbs at regular intervals. It worked. Cattle that pushed through smooth wire were deterred by the painful barbs. Within a decade, millions of miles of barbed wire crisscrossed the plains. The invention was simple enough that dozens of competitors developed variations - different barb designs, different wire gauges, different spacing. Each variety tells a story of competition and patent disputes.

sections.title: The Transformation
sections.body: Barbed wire ended the open range. Before fencing, cattle from different ranches mixed freely on public land, sorted during annual roundups. Cowboys drove herds hundreds of miles to railheads. The land was common. Barbed wire made private property enforceable for the first time in the West. Ranchers enclosed their land; farmers protected crops from wandering cattle. The great cattle drives ended - fences blocked the trails. Cowboys became fence riders, patrolling wire rather than herding cattle across open country. The West was tamed, subdivided, and owned. The transformation took barely a generation.

sections.title: The Conflicts
sections.body: Not everyone welcomed the wire. Cowboys cut fences that blocked traditional trails. 'Fence cutting wars' erupted across Texas and other states. Large ranchers fenced in water sources, killing smaller operations. Native Americans watched their remaining lands subdivided. The wire carried a cost in blood as well - cattle caught in fences died of wounds or infection; horses were scarred; people handling wire were cut constantly. The name 'devil's rope' captured the ambivalence: necessary but cruel, transformative but destructive. The museum displays both the wire and the tools for cutting it.

sections.title: The Collectors
sections.body: Barbed wire collecting is a serious hobby. Over 2,000 patented varieties exist, each with different barb designs, wire configurations, and manufacturing quirks. Rare early varieties can sell for hundreds of dollars per 18-inch strand. Collectors trade, display, and argue about authenticity. The hobby has its own organization (the California Barbed Wire Collectors Association), its own shows, and its own terminology. The Devil's Rope Museum is both historical archive and collector's mecca - displaying rare varieties, explaining identification, and connecting enthusiasts. The obsessive cataloging of slight variations in something as utilitarian as fencing wire is itself a kind of American folk art.

sections.title: Visiting the Devil's Rope Museum
sections.body: The Devil's Rope Museum is located at 100 Kingsley Street in McLean, Texas, along old Route 66 (now I-40 frontage). The museum displays over 2,000 barbed wire varieties, along with fencing tools, ranch equipment, and Route 66 memorabilia. Admission is free; donations support operations. The museum building was once a brassiere factory - another piece of Texas roadside history. McLean itself is a classic Route 66 town, small and quiet since the interstate bypassed it. Amarillo, 75 miles west, has the nearest significant services. Amarillo's Rick Husband International Airport is the closest commercial airport. The museum is open limited hours; call ahead to confirm.

content.flightContext: Located at 35.23°N, 100.60°W in the Texas Panhandle, along the I-40 corridor. From altitude, McLean appears as a small town beside the interstate, with the old Route 66 alignment visible as a parallel road. The terrain is flat High Plains - wheat fields, ranches, and the endless horizontal that barbed wire made ownable. Amarillo is 75 miles west. The landscape represents exactly what barbed wire transformed: open prairie that was once unfenceable, now divided into neat rectangles. Rick Husband International Airport in Amarillo is the nearest commercial service.
